headline: Trump said no. Oil is back above $107.
standfirst: Friday closed the first winning week in three — the S&P 500 rose 0.51% to 7,743.41, the Dow 0.93% to 51,828.62 and the Nasdaq 0.48% to 27,068.72 — because Iran's foreign minister offered to reopen Hormuz within seven days, Brent settled 2.1% lower at $104.32 and the ten-year came back from a 5.228% high, its highest since 2007, to about 5.17%. On Saturday Trump rejected the offer; on Sunday he said indirect talks continue this week and further strikes remain possible. By 05:44 UTC Brent is $107.58, up 3.12%, WTI $94.66, gold $4,216 and at its lowest since early August, the Kospi down 2.5% and S&P futures 0.2–0.3% lower. It is jobs-and-inflation week — the RBA on Tuesday, PCE and quarter-end on Wednesday, ISM on Thursday, payrolls on Friday — with October about 65% priced for a second Fed hike, down from 71% on Thursday.

bullets.title: The offer, the rejection, and the $3 it cost
bullets.text: On Friday at the UN, Iran's foreign minister Araghchi said the Strait of Hormuz would reopen and nuclear talks restart within seven days if Washington met Tehran's conditions: an end to the naval blockade of Iranian ports, the lifting of oil sanctions, the release of frozen assets and a halt to hostilities including in Lebanon — the terms of the June memorandum that collapsed. Brent settled at $104.32, down 2.1%, and WTI at $92.41, down 2.3%, and US stocks rallied into the close. On Saturday the Wall Street Journal reported Trump had rejected the proposal and told aides strikes could resume after November's midterms; Trump confirmed it — “they made a proposal but I rejected it” — and said Tehran wants a deal because it is “losing so badly”. On Sunday he told Axios indirect talks continue this week and, asked about new strikes, said that is always under consideration; Araghchi told NBC Iran is ready for a “doomsday war” but the door to diplomacy is open, and Iran's president told CBS there would be no talks under coercion. The Revolutionary Guard claimed it seized a US unmanned underwater vessel in the strait; the Saudi-led coalition intercepted Houthi projectiles; Qatar is still mediating. Brent was $105.90 at 21:40 ET Sunday and $107.58 by 05:44 UTC. Two supply-side footnotes: Baker Hughes counted 599 active US rigs, up four, a third straight weekly rise and the most since May 2024, and one report put September Hormuz flows at 7.4 million barrels a day as Saudi cargoes were rerouted. Trump is reportedly due to make an Oval Office announcement on Monday afternoon.

bullets.title: Friday's data: expectations at 4.6%, orders flat, capex up 1.6%
bullets.text: Durable goods orders were unchanged in August against −0.4% expected, with July revised up to +0.9%; ex-transport rose 0.3% against 0.6%; core capital goods orders rose 1.6% against 0.5%, with July revised from flat to +0.6%. Michigan's final September sentiment was 48.1 — above 47.6 expected and the 47.8 preliminary, but down from 51.7 in August and the lowest in four months — and one-year inflation expectations were confirmed at 4.6%, up from 4.0% a month earlier, with five-year at 3.4%. The expectations line did the damage: the ten-year hit 5.228% on the release, its highest since 2007, and the thirty-year went through 5.5% for the first time since 2004; both eased as oil fell, the ten-year to about 5.15–5.18% and the two-year to 4.862%. Thirty-year mortgage rates are above 7%. CME futures now price October at 64–66% after 71% on Thursday and December at about 80%, with roughly 88bp of tightening over the next year; a Bloomberg survey of 173 respondents found 53% expect the thirty-year above 6% within the year, and a global bond index yield went above 4% last week for the first time since 2007.

bullets.title: Dollar, yen, sterling: three central banks' worth of jawboning
bullets.text: The dollar index is at 101.39, a two-month high and its first back-to-back weekly gain since June; the euro is $1.1383, down 2% on the month. The yen is the exception. On Friday Japan's finance minister Katayama said Trump had raised the weak yen with Prime Minister Takaichi at their 22 September summit, Takaichi called an undervalued yen a problem, and Katayama said she is in currency dialogue with the US Treasury; USD/JPY fell from Thursday's three-week high of 159.04 to 156.94 in New York, closed at 157.22, and is 157.75 this morning. BBH puts the range at 155–160 with the Fed at 3.75–4.00% against the BoJ's 1.25%. Sterling is $1.3240, just above three-month lows, after Governor Bailey told an Oxford conference that “it's going to get harder to maintain that stance the longer we have high energy prices” and that the Bank cannot wait for full evidence on expectations, though pass-through so far is “quite subdued”. The MPC held 6–3 at 3.75% on 17 September; three deputy governors have since moved towards hikes; the market prices about 80% for November and more than four quarter-points over the next year, with the Bank itself forecasting inflation slightly above 4% in early 2027. UK police arrested five men near an air base used in US strikes on Iran. Ramsden speaks on QT at 12:00 ET today and Lagarde testifies to the European Parliament.

bullets.title: Asia opened the week lower; the RBA hikes tomorrow
bullets.text: The Kospi fell about 2.5% in its first session after the Chuseok holiday, with Samsung and SK Hynix down more than 4%; the CSI 300 lost about 2% and the Shanghai Composite 1.5%, leaving Chinese blue chips more than 5% lower on the month; the Nikkei opened higher and gave it back to finish flat; Hong Kong rose 0.8%; the ASX 200 was little changed. India's Nifty fell 1.25% to 22,855, below 23,000, and the Sensex 1.3%, with a three-day nationwide bank strike starting today and the rupee at 95.88. Gold is $4,192–4,216 depending on the print, down more than 2% and the lowest since 5 August; Bitcoin is about $83,100, down 1.6%, with roughly 70,000 accounts liquidated overnight. The Reserve Bank of Australia decides at 04:30 UTC on Tuesday — 00:30 ET — with ASX futures pricing about 90% for a 25bp hike to 4.60%, the fourth of 2026 and the highest cash rate in 15 years. NAB, CBA, ANZ and BofA all forecast it; ANZ expects a split vote and another in November to 4.85%; BofA expects unanimity. Governor Bullock said last week that unemployment, 4.6% in August, may need to rise to bring inflation back to target; UBS thinks about 5%. Wednesday's monthly CPI is seen 4.1% after 3.5%. AUD/USD is $0.70, up 5.15% on the year.

bullets.title: The week: PCE and quarter-end Wednesday, ISM Thursday, payrolls Friday
bullets.text: Tuesday: JOLTS openings seen 7.23 million after 7.27 million; Conference Board confidence seen 90.0 after 89.4, the lowest since January; Musalem at 07:30 ET, Goolsbee at 13:00, Williams at 14:00. Wednesday is quarter-end and the heaviest day: ADP seen 70,000 after 38,000; core PCE seen +0.3% on the month and 3.4% on the year after 0.2% and 3.3%, headline seen +0.4% after 3.7% year on year in July; personal spending +0.8%; final Q2 GDP nudged to 1.6% from 1.5%; Chicago PMI 51.3 after 47.1; overnight China's NBS PMI seen 50.1 after 49.8, Australian CPI, German CPI seen +0.5% on the month, UK final GDP; Micron after the close with earnings seen at $31.45 a share against $3.03 a year ago and options implying a 9% move; Kashkari at 18:00 ET; the Tankan at 19:50 ET seen 25 after 22. Thursday: Swiss CPI after 0.8%; ISM manufacturing seen 54.8 after 54.6 with prices paid 72.0 after 71.1; claims seen 199,000; Williams at 15:30 ET; Nike after the close; Tokyo CPI at 19:30 ET; Chinese markets shut for Golden Week. Friday 2 October: euro-area flash HICP seen 3.5% after 3.2% with core 2.6% after 2.4%; September payrolls seen 100,000 after 162,000 — Barclays is at 50,000 and expects August revised down — with unemployment seen 4.2% after 4.1% and hourly earnings +0.3%. Chair Warsh has said the labour side of the mandate is in “good shape”; Goolsbee has said hiking into a supply shock is “painful”. Then the FOMC minutes on 7 October, the ten- and thirty-year auctions on 7 and 8, JPMorgan on the 13th and CPI on the 14th.

calendar.note: The only US release of the day. The regional surveys have run hot since the flash PMI's 57.0, and Dallas is the oil-patch one.

calendar.event: BoE's Ramsden on QT; Lagarde at the European Parliament
calendar.note: Ramsden three days after Bailey's “harder to hold” line, with November about 80% priced. Lagarde's quarterly hearing, time not fixed, four days before a flash HICP seen at 3.5%.

calendar.event: Fed's Barkin speaks; Jefferies after the close
calendar.note: The first Fed voice since Friday's 4.6% expectations print and the weekend's oil move. Jefferies is the first look at trading and banking revenue through the quarter the Fed turned.
About 90% priced for 25bp to 4.60%. The hike is the consensus; whether Bullock leaves November open is the trade.
Openings seen 7.23 million; confidence seen 90.0 after 89.4. Musalem 07:30, Goolsbee 13:00, Williams 14:00 ET.

calendar.event: PCE (August); final Q2 GDP; ADP 08:15; quarter-end
calendar.note: Core PCE seen 0.3% on the month and 3.4% on the year after 3.3%. The print the Fed named, on the day quarter-end rebalancing flows are largest. Micron after the close, Kashkari at 18:00 ET.

calendar.event: ISM manufacturing (September); Nike after the close
calendar.note: Seen 54.8 after 54.6 with prices paid 72.0. The flash PMI said 57.0; a matching ISM confirms the repricing. China shuts for Golden Week.
Seen 100,000 after 162,000, unemployment 4.2%, earnings +0.3%. With October at 65%, a strong print removes the last doubt; a weak one is the only thing on the calendar that could take the hike away.

sessionNote: Monday's tape is a headline market with almost no data: S&P futures are 0.2–0.3% lower, Brent is up 3% and back above $107, gold is down 2.4%, the dollar is at a two-month high, and Asia is mixed to lower with Korea off 2.5%. The schedule is the Dallas Fed at 10:30 ET, Barkin at 13:30, a reported Oval Office announcement in the afternoon, and Iran talks pencilled for “this week” with no time. There is no coupon supply all week, so the bond market has nothing to clear until PCE on Wednesday. The cleanest read is the ten-year against Friday's 5.228% high — equities rallied when it backed away and stalled when it tested it — and oil into the afternoon headline is the other. Nothing forces a move before the RBA at 00:30 ET on Tuesday; whatever happens today is positioning for the week, not a reaction to a print, and should be sized as such.
watchOut: Trading the Iran headline as if it were new. Friday's rally was built on a seven-day proposal that was rejected within 24 hours; Monday's oil bid is built on the rejection and a promise of talks “this week”. Both sides have now said the same thing twice — Tehran's conditions are unchanged, Washington's are unchanged — and Brent has moved $3 each way on the repetition. The trap is sizing for a resolution when the tape is pricing a schedule: an announcement this afternoon, indirect talks midweek, and a payrolls print on Friday that only matters if it is weak. The second trap is quarter-end. Wednesday's PCE lands on the day rebalancing flows out of what rose into what fell are largest, and a move that looks like a reaction to the inflation number may be a pension fund selling what went up.

archive.headline: The week the Treasury market stopped waiting for the Fed
archive.summary: Weekend edition. The ten-year went from 4.95% to 5.21% in a week on a 58.4 flash PMI, three auctions at two-decade highs and eight Fed speakers, and every Treasury from two years out cleared 5%. Equities held on Meta and AMD while the Dow fell for a fourth week, Brent round-tripped $100–$99–$106 on Iran, and October was 71% priced for a second hike.

archive.headline: A survey took the ten-year to 5.11%. An auction kept it there.
archive.summary: A flash composite PMI of 58.4, the highest since July 2021, took the ten-year up 14.6bp to 5.116% — its worst day since April 2025 — and a $70 billion five-year auction stopped at 5.033%, the highest since 2006. Barr said further hikes were likely needed and October went to 73% priced; every sector but energy fell and Brent rose back above $100.

archive.headline: The Fed said “we’ll see”. The two-year auction said 4.787%.
archive.summary: Treasury sold $69 billion of two-years at 4.787%, the highest stop since May 2024, on demand that held; Brent settled at $99.25 for its first close under $100 since 9 September; four Fed officials, none voting this year, all leaned toward more. The Nasdaq closed at a second straight record while financials fell 1.97%.

archive.headline: An App Store ranking moved a trillion dollars
archive.summary: Meta's Muse agent topped the US iPhone chart and the CPU complex repriced around it: Meta +11.43%, AMD +9.95% to a first $1 trillion close, Intel +12%, Arm +17%, and the Nasdaq to its first record since June. Crude fell to an eleven-day low on Hormuz shipping data and the ten-year came back under 5%, into a $69 billion two-year auction.

archive.headline: The war premium leaks out before the UN
archive.summary: Monday with no US data and a live diplomatic wire. Crude fell for a fourth session as traders priced a chance of US–Iran contact at the UN General Assembly and Saudi Arabia worked to restore its East–West pipeline, with the ten-year coming into the day at 5.01% after its first close above 5% since July 2007.

archive.headline: The hike landed. The bond market blinked first.
archive.summary: Weekend edition. The Fed's unanimous 25bp on Wednesday took the Dow down 631 points and Thursday gave most of it back, with the S&P up 1.14% to 7,637.76 as the ten-year fell to 4.93% and oil slid. The weekend risk was the Iran war, with Trump saying he was near a decision on resuming large-scale strikes.

archive.headline: The ten-year touched 5% into the decision. The hike is not the event.
archive.summary: FOMC day. The 10-year had closed at 5.00% after touching 5.04%, the highest since 2007, with a 25bp hike priced at 92–94%. WTI had jumped 5.1% to $106.56 as fighting intensified in the Middle East; every US sector but energy closed red on Tuesday.
